questions.question: White to move: The Black King on g8 is trapped behind its own pawns! Find Checkmate in 1 move!
questions.explanation: 1. Ra8# is the classic Back-Rank Mate! Black's own pawns on f7, g7, and h7 block the King from escaping.
questions.hintText: Your rook can zoom to the back row. Look at where the Black King is stuck!

questions.question: White to move: Use your Queen and King to deliver Checkmate in 1 move!
questions.explanation: 1. Qa8# is mate! The Queen checks along the top row and covers e8 and g8, while the White King on f6 guards e7, f7 and g7.
questions.hintText: Your Queen can reach the top row. Your King already guards the squares next to Black's King.

questions.question: Which word is the OPPOSITE (antonym) of 'ANCIENT' (very, very old)?
questions.explanation: 'Ancient' means from a very long time ago, so its opposite (antonym) is 'Modern' (new, from today).
questions.hintText: Ancient pyramids are old; today's cities are...

questions.question: If a turtle walks at a 'SLUGGISH' pace, how is the turtle moving?
questions.optionsString: Very slowly|Super fast|Backwards|High in the sky
questions.explanation: 'Sluggish' (like a garden slug!) means moving very slowly and with low energy.
questions.hintText: Think of how fast a little slug or snail moves!

questions.question: You program a toy robot with the block: [REPEAT 4 TIMES: Jump 3 steps forward]. How many steps does the robot jump in total?
questions.explanation: A repeat loop runs the instruction 4 times: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 4 × 3 = 12 steps forward!
questions.hintText: Picture 4 jumps in a row and add up the steps of every jump.

questions.question: Your robot faces NORTH. You run: [Turn Right 90°] then [Turn Right 90°] again. Which direction is the robot facing now?
questions.explanation: Facing North → Turn Right once faces East (90°) → Turn Right a second time faces South (180° opposite)!
questions.hintText: Draw a compass. Turn right once, then once more.

questions.question: In standard chess valuation, how many points is a Rook worth?
questions.explanation: Pawn = 1, Knight/Bishop = 3, Rook = 5, Queen = 9.
questions.hintText: A pawn is worth 1. A rook is stronger than a bishop but weaker than a queen.

questions.question: Which word means the same as 'GIGANTIC'?
questions.explanation: 'Gigantic' and 'Enormous' both describe something exceptionally huge.
questions.hintText: The word starts like 'giant'. How big is a giant?

questions.question: Your robot is at square (0, 0). It executes [MOVE FORWARD 2], then [MOVE FORWARD 3]. How many squares did it move?
questions.explanation: 2 + 3 = 5 squares total.
questions.hintText: Both moves go the same way, so put them together.

questions.question: Which piece moves in an 'L-shape' (two squares one way, then one square perpendicular) and can jump over other pieces?
questions.explanation: The Knight moves in an L-shape and is the only piece that can jump over others.
questions.hintText: Shaped like a horse.

questions.question: What is the direct antonym (opposite) of 'BRAVE'?
questions.explanation: The opposite of brave is cowardly (fearful).
questions.hintText: A hero is brave; someone who runs away in fear is...

questions.question: In code, if a statement says `IF is_raining == True: take_umbrella() ELSE: wear_sunglasses()`. If it is SUNNY outside, what do you do?
questions.explanation: Since is_raining is False, the code enters the ELSE block: wear_sunglasses().
questions.hintText: On a sunny day, is 'is_raining' true or false? Then see which part of the code runs.

questions.question: What do we call a double attack where one piece, often a Knight, attacks TWO enemy pieces at once?
questions.explanation: A fork is a tactical maneuver where a single piece (often a Knight) attacks two enemy pieces at once.
questions.hintText: Think of a tool for eating at dinner: it has several points that poke at once.

questions.question: Which of these words is made of TWO words joined together?
questions.explanation: Butterfly is formed from 'butter' and 'fly'.
questions.hintText: Find a word you can split into two smaller words you already know.

questions.question: A drawing program repeats: [DRAW LINE, TURN 45°] 8 times. What shape does it draw?
questions.explanation: 8 sides × 45° = 360°, forming a complete 8-sided regular Octagon.
questions.hintText: 8 repetitions create an 8-sided shape.

questions.question: How many total squares are on a standard 8×8 chessboard?
questions.explanation: 8 rows × 8 columns = 64 squares (32 light and 32 dark).
questions.hintText: Count by 8s once for each row of the board.

questions.question: What is an antonym for 'FREEZE'?
questions.explanation: The opposite of freeze is melt.
questions.hintText: Ice freezes; when it gets warm, it...

questions.question: You store `apples = 5`. Then you execute `apples = apples + 3`. What is the value stored in apples now?
questions.hintText: Picture a basket with 5 apples. The code puts in 3 more. Count them all.

questions.question: What is a 'PIN' in chess?
questions.optionsString: A piece that cannot move without exposing a bigger piece|Two pawns bump into each other head on and block the way|A pawn that reaches the last row and becomes a Queen|Moving two knights at the same time in a single turn
questions.explanation: A pin prevents an enemy piece from moving because doing so would expose the King or Queen behind it.
questions.hintText: Think of a pin holding paper on a wall: it can't wiggle away.

questions.question: What does 'SWIFT' mean?
questions.explanation: 'Swift' means moving or capable of moving with great speed.
questions.hintText: A swift runner is the first to cross the finish line.

questions.question: A bug in computer programming is:
questions.optionsString: A mistake in a program's code|A real beetle in the keyboard|A trick that makes games faster|A new kind of computer mouse
questions.explanation: A bug is an unintentional coding flaw or logic error in software.
questions.hintText: Programmers 'debug' their code. What are they looking for and fixing?

questions.question: Can a King EVER move to a square attacked by an enemy piece?
questions.optionsString: Yes, but only if it has no other move|No, never: that is moving into check|Yes, but only on the first move of the game|Only if it is capturing a Queen
questions.explanation: Moving the King into check is strictly illegal in chess.
questions.hintText: What would happen if your King stood on a square an enemy piece attacks?

questions.question: The prefix 'TELE-' (in telephone, telescope, television) comes from Greek and means:
questions.explanation: Greek 'tele' means far or distant (seeing far, hearing far).
questions.hintText: A telephone lets you talk to a friend who is not in the same room.

questions.question: To make a sandwich, which step MUST come first?
questions.optionsString: Eat the sandwich|Take two slices of bread|Put the plate in the dishwasher|Wrap the sandwich in foil
questions.explanation: Algorithms require strict logical order: you must get the bread before making the sandwich.
questions.hintText: Think of the steps in order. Which one needs nothing before it?

questions.question: What special pawn capture can ONLY happen immediately after an enemy pawn moves two squares forward from its starting rank?
questions.explanation: En Passant allows a pawn to capture an adjacent enemy pawn that just moved two squares past it.
questions.hintText: It has a French name. Your pawn captures as if the enemy pawn moved only one step.

questions.question: A comparison that uses the words 'like' or 'as' (e.g. 'brave as a lion') is called a:
questions.explanation: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'.
questions.hintText: Think of the word 'similar': the two things are alike.

questions.question: `count = 0; REPEAT 4 TIMES: count = count + 2`. What is count at the end?
questions.explanation: 4 repetitions × 2 = 8.
questions.hintText: Start at 0 and count up in 2s, once for every repeat.

questions.question: A 'SKEWER' is like a reverse pin: which piece is attacked in FRONT?
questions.optionsString: A pawn, with a Queen standing behind it|A piece that is worth less than the piece behind it|A piece that is worth more than the piece behind it|A piece that is worth exactly the same as the one behind
questions.explanation: In a skewer, the more valuable piece (e.g. King or Queen) is in front and is forced to move, exposing a piece behind.
questions.hintText: Picture a kebab stick going through two pieces in a line.

questions.question: What does the popular idiom 'A piece of cake' mean?
questions.optionsString: A tasty dessert from a bakery|Something that is very easy to do|A very hard homework task|An expensive birthday present
questions.explanation: 'A piece of cake' is an English idiom meaning an effortless, very easy task.
questions.hintText: It isn't about food. Think of a job you can do without any trouble.

questions.question: A robot starts facing East. Which command turns it to face North?
questions.optionsString: Turn Left 90°|Turn Right 90°|Turn Around 180°|Move Forward 1 step
questions.explanation: Facing East (right), turning counter-clockwise (Left 90°) points directly to North (up).
questions.hintText: Draw a compass: East is on the right and North is at the top. Which way do you turn?

questions.question: What is STALEMATE in chess?
questions.optionsString: The King is in check and has no escape (a loss)|A player has no legal move and is NOT in check (a draw)|A pawn is promoted to a Knight on the last row|A player's time on the clock runs out
questions.explanation: Stalemate occurs when the player to move has no legal moves and their King is NOT in check; the game ends in an immediate DRAW.
questions.hintText: Ask two questions: is the King attacked, and can any piece move?

questions.question: Which word is an ADJECTIVE (describes a noun)?
questions.explanation: 'Playful' is an adjective (e.g. a playful puppy). 'Play' is a verb, 'Quickly' an adverb, 'Player' a noun.
questions.hintText: Which word fits in 'The ___ puppy ran home'?

questions.question: Computers store all photos, sounds, and games using binary digits (bits). What TWO numbers make up binary?
questions.explanation: Binary code is base-2, using only the digits 0 and 1 (off and on).
questions.hintText: Think of a light switch: it has only two settings.

packs.title: Grandmaster Chess Endgames & Tactics
packs.subtitle: Interactive 2D FEN mating nets, forks, pins & sacrifices
packs.author: QuizLock Chess Lab

questions.question: White to move: Deliver Opera Box Mate in 1 with the Rook on d1 supported by the Bishop on g5!
questions.explanation: Paul Morphy's Opera Game motif: 1. Rd8# mates the Black King because the g5 Bishop protects d8!
questions.hintText: Check along the open file where your Bishop stops the King from capturing the Rook.

questions.question: White to move: Execute Boden's Criss-Cross Bishop Checkmate in 1!
questions.explanation: 1. Ba6# checks along the a6-c8 diagonal while the f4 Bishop covers c7 and b8 and the Rook covers d7!
questions.hintText: The two Bishops work together: one gives check, the other seals the King's escape squares.

questions.question: White to move: Epaulette Mate! Black's King on e8 is flanked by its own two Rooks on d8 and f8. Deliver mate with the Queen!
questions.explanation: 1. Qe6# is Epaulette Mate! Black's own rooks on d8 and f8 act like shoulder pads blocking escape.
questions.hintText: Find the check that also covers both squares diagonally in front of the King.

questions.question: White to move: Anastasia's Mate! Knight on e7 controls g8 and g6; slide the Rook to the h-file for mate!
questions.explanation: 1. Rh3# completes Anastasia's Mate—the Knight on e7 takes away g8 and g6 while Black's g7 pawn blocks the King.
questions.hintText: Check along an open file: the Knight and the pawn already box in the King.

questions.question: What piece delivers the final checkmate in a classic Smothered Mate while the enemy King is surrounded by its own pieces?
questions.explanation: A Knight jumps over pieces to deliver checkmate to a trapped King boxed in by its own army.
questions.hintText: Only one piece can leap over the pieces crowding the King to give check.

questions.question: In a King and Pawn endgame, what critical concept involves placing your King directly opposite the enemy King with one square between them?
questions.explanation: The Opposition is a fundamental weapon to outflank the enemy King and escort your pawn to promotion.
questions.hintText: A battle over who has to move: the Kings face each other and one must give way.

questions.question: In the famous Lucena Rook endgame, what is the key tactical technique used to shield the King from vertical checks?
questions.optionsString: Underpromotion to Knight|Perpetual check|Building a bridge with the Rook (on the 4th rank)|Stalemate trick
questions.explanation: The 'Bridge Building' technique uses the Rook on the 4th rank (e.g. Rd4) to block checks and allow the pawn to promote.
questions.hintText: Your own Rook can step in front of the checks and act as a shield.

questions.question: How does the defending player draw a Rook and Pawn endgame in Philidor's 3rd-rank defense?
questions.optionsString: Keep the Rook on the 6th/3rd rank until the pawn advances, then check relentlessly from behind|Sacrifice the Rook immediately|Attack the enemy King from the side|Trade rooks immediately
questions.explanation: The defending Rook holds the 6th (or 3rd) rank cutting off the King. When the pawn pushes, the Rook checks from behind.
questions.hintText: Block the enemy King's path first; the checks only start once the pawn has advanced.

questions.question: What famous sacrifice involves offering a Bishop on h7 (or h2) with check to strip the castled King's shelter?
questions.optionsString: Damiano's Mate|Greek Gift Sacrifice (Bxh7+)|Blackburne's Mate|Legal's Mate
questions.explanation: The Greek Gift (Bxh7+) tears open the King's defense, followed by Ng5+ and Qh5.
questions.hintText: Think of the ancient story where a 'gift' let the enemy inside the walls.

questions.question: What does the German chess term 'Zugzwang' mean?
questions.optionsString: A rapid counter-attack|A perpetual sequence of checks|Compulsion to move, where any legal move worsens the player's position|A sudden discovered checkmate
questions.explanation: Zugzwang is a situation where obligation to make a move leads to disadvantage or defeat.
questions.hintText: Think of a position where you wish you could simply pass the move.

questions.question: The 'Rule of the Square' allows a player to instantly determine what without calculation?
questions.optionsString: Whether castling is legally permitted|Whether a defending King can catch a passed pawn before it promotes|If a bishop can control two diagonals|How many rooks are active
questions.explanation: If the defending King can step inside the square of the passed pawn, it can catch and stop the pawn.
questions.hintText: Square drawn from the pawn to its promotion square.

questions.question: In a 3 vs 3 pawn endgame on three adjacent files, which pawn advance starts the decisive breakthrough?
questions.optionsString: A flank pawn advance|Pushing the central pawn (e.g. b6) to create open passed paths|Retreating the king|Moving the a-pawn
questions.explanation: Pushing the middle pawn sacrifices it to force a capture, enabling an immediate push of the other pawns to queen.
questions.hintText: Give up one pawn so that a neighboring pawn becomes passed.

questions.question: When is an endgame with opposite-colored bishops notoriously prone to end in a draw?
questions.optionsString: Even when one side is down one or two pawns, because the defender establishes an impenetrable blockade on their color|Only when all pawns are traded|Never, opposite bishops always produce decisive wins|Only on move 50
questions.explanation: Opposite-colored bishops cannot challenge each other, enabling the defender to set up unbreakable color blockades.
questions.hintText: Each bishop stays on its own color: can they ever attack each other?

questions.question: What is a 'Windmill' tactic (such as in the famous Torre vs Lasker game)?
questions.optionsString: Spinning the rooks across all 4 corners|A repetitive sequence of discovered checks and regular checks using a Rook and Bishop to win multiple pieces|Promoting three pawns in consecutive turns|A perpetual queen sacrifice
questions.explanation: A windmill uses alternating discovered checks and direct checks with Rook and Bishop to vacuum up the opponent's pieces.
questions.hintText: Picture a windmill's sails turning: the same two pieces repeat a pattern again and again.

questions.question: What is the purpose of King triangulation in endgames?
questions.optionsString: To move across all three central files|To attack the enemy Queen from three directions|To lose a tempo and return to the original square, transferring the move to the opponent and putting them in zugzwang|To force stalemate
questions.explanation: Triangulation is a 3-move triangular King maneuver that wastes a tempo to hand the turn to the opponent.
questions.hintText: A short detour with the King can change who has to move.

questions.question: In Queen vs pawn-on-the-7th endings (defender's King near the pawn, enemy King far away), which pawns can still draw?
questions.optionsString: Knight and Central pawns (b, d, e, g pawns)|Rook pawns (a, h) and Bishop pawns (c, f)|Only the d-pawn|No pawn can draw against a Queen
questions.explanation: Rook pawns (a, h) and Bishop pawns (c, f) have stalemate resources in the corner, preventing the Queen from winning.
questions.hintText: Think about where the defender's King can hide in a corner to create stalemate.

questions.question: What was Richard Réti's genius concept in his 1921 study featuring a white King chasing two distant pawns?
questions.optionsString: The King moves along a diagonal, simultaneously threatening to support its own passed pawn AND intercept the enemy pawn|Sacrificing the King for a stalemate|Promoting to a bishop|Underpromoting to a knight
questions.explanation: Réti's diagonal King walk exploits Euclidean vs chessboard metric: walking diagonally closes distance to two separate goals simultaneously.
questions.hintText: Compare how many King moves each goal needs, then look for one path that serves both.

questions.question: White has a King, a light-squared Bishop and an h-pawn. What is the theoretical result if Black's King reaches h8?
questions.optionsString: White wins easily|It is a dead theoretical DRAW|Black wins|Loss on time
questions.explanation: The light-squared Bishop can never control the dark promotion square h8, so the defending King just shuffles between h8 and g8 and every attempt to dislodge it leads to stalemate.
questions.hintText: Compare the color of the Bishop's squares with the color of the corner square.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of moves required to checkmate with Bishop and Knight against a lone King from any position with best play?
questions.explanation: Under optimal play, Bishop and Knight mate can take up to 33 moves to drive the King into the corner matching the Bishop's color.
questions.hintText: The longest of the basic mates; a Knight 'W-maneuver' herds the King to the right corner.

questions.question: Which other endgame type are pure Knight and Pawn endgames most mathematically similar to?
questions.optionsString: Rook endgames|Pure King and Pawn endgames|Queen endgames|Bishop endgames
questions.explanation: Because Knights are short-range and cannot lose a tempo, pure Knight endgames closely mirror pure pawn endgames.
questions.hintText: Think of an ending with only short-range moves, where the fight is over key squares.

questions.question: What did Siegbert Tarrasch famously state regarding the placement of Rooks in endgames?
questions.optionsString: Rooks belong behind passed pawns — both behind your own to support them, and behind enemy pawns to halt them|Rooks should always stay on the starting rank|Rooks must capture bishops immediately|Rooks must avoid open files
questions.explanation: Tarrasch's rule: Place rooks behind passed pawns to maximize mobility as the pawn advances.
questions.hintText: Where does a Rook keep the most open lines while a passed pawn advances?

questions.question: Can a lone King and Rook force checkmate against a lone King?
questions.optionsString: No, it is a theoretical draw|Only if the King is trapped in the center|Yes, it is a basic fundamental checkmate|Only with pawns present
questions.explanation: King and Rook vs King is an elementary forced checkmate, pushing the King to any edge of the board.
questions.hintText: Recall the basic mates that every beginner learns first: what do they use?

questions.question: What is a 'Clearance Sacrifice' in grandmaster play?
questions.optionsString: Sacrificing a piece to clean the entire board|Sacrificing a piece specifically to vacate a square, file, or diagonal for a more deadly attacking piece|Resigning with grace|Trading queens in opening
questions.explanation: A clearance sacrifice frees a vital square or line (e.g. vacating f7 for a queen entry).
questions.hintText: Ask what the sacrificed piece was blocking.

questions.question: What is a 'Fortress' in chess endgames?
questions.optionsString: A defensive setup where the weaker side creates an impenetrable barrier that the opponent cannot break despite material advantage|Surrounding the King with 4 rooks|A double castling structure|A pawn chain stretching from a1 to h8
questions.explanation: A fortress is a theoretical draw where material superiority cannot breach the defensive perimeter.
questions.hintText: Think of a position where having extra material still cannot make progress.

questions.question: What is the tactical distinction between 'Deflection' and 'Decoy'?
questions.optionsString: They are exact synonyms with no distinction|Deflection forces a defending piece AWAY from a vital square, while Decoy lures an enemy piece ONTO a fatal square|Decoy is only used with pawns|Deflection only applies to the King
questions.explanation: Deflection removes a defender from duty; decoy pulls a piece onto a doomed square.
questions.hintText: To deflect is to turn aside; a decoy is a lure. Compare what each does to the piece.

questions.question: In Queen vs Rook endgame (Philidor position), what is the optimal result with best play?
questions.optionsString: Always a draw|Rook always wins|Queen wins by forcing zugzwang and winning the Rook|Loss by repetition
questions.explanation: Queen vs Rook is a forced win for the Queen, though technically demanding to execute without allowing stalemate.
questions.hintText: Compare the values of the two pieces, then ask whether the weaker side can hold.

questions.question: In the endgame, why does the King transform from a vulnerable target into an aggressive attacking piece?
questions.optionsString: Because check is no longer allowed in endgames|With few pieces remaining, the danger of checkmate drops dramatically, making the King an indispensable active fighter|The King gains the movement powers of a Queen|Pawns protect the King automatically
questions.explanation: As mating material decreases, the King must actively control central squares and assist passed pawns.
questions.hintText: Think about how many pieces are left to attack the King.

questions.question: What is a 'Zwischenzug' in tactical combinations?
questions.optionsString: An 'in-between' unexpected move that changes the tactical evaluation before an expected recapture|Surrendering early|Offering a draw on move 1|A double pawn push
questions.explanation: A Zwischenzug inserts an intermediate threat (like check or counter-attack) before completing the expected line.
questions.hintText: Split the word: 'zwischen' + 'Zug'. Think about timing.

questions.question: What is an 'Isolated Pawn' and what is its primary endgame weakness?
questions.optionsString: A pawn with no enemy pawns ahead of it|A pawn with no friendly pawns on adjacent files; it cannot be defended by another pawn and requires piece babysitting|A pawn on the e-file|A pawn that moved three squares
questions.explanation: An isolated pawn cannot be defended by fellow pawns, becoming a chronic target in endgames.
questions.hintText: 'Isolated' means cut off: look at which pawns are missing next to it.

questions.question: What does it mean when a piece is 'Overloaded' in tactical calculations?
questions.optionsString: It weighs too much physically|It has moved more than 20 times|It is tasked with defending two critical squares/pieces at the same time and cannot cover both|It is surrounded by 8 pieces
questions.explanation: An overloaded piece has multiple defensive duties; attacking one duty distracts it from the other.
questions.hintText: Count how many jobs the piece has to do at the same time.

questions.question: Why is the 'Bishop Pair' generally considered a significant long-term strategic advantage in open positions?
questions.optionsString: Because they can jump over pawns|Together they control both light and dark squares across the entire board, cutting swaths of open diagonals|They can castle together|They promote to two Queens simultaneously
questions.explanation: Two bishops complement each other, covering every square color on open boards where diagonals are clear.
questions.hintText: Think about the square color a single bishop can never reach.

questions.question: Why is a discovered check often so devastatingly powerful?
questions.optionsString: The moving piece can attack any target (even a Queen) while the unveiled piece simultaneously checks the King|It counts as two turns in a row|The opponent must surrender their Queen|The King cannot run away
questions.explanation: Because the King MUST respond to the check, the moving piece can capture material with complete impunity.
questions.hintText: The King must answer the check; what is the other piece free to do meanwhile?

questions.question: Why is a Rook invading the 7th rank (the 'Pig on the 7th') so prized in master play?
questions.optionsString: It promotes to Queen immediately|It attacks unmoved enemy pawns horizontally, pins the enemy King to the back rank, and creates deadly mating nets|It prevents all pawn moves|It doubles in value to 10 points
questions.explanation: The 7th rank is the home of vulnerable enemy pawns and clamps down on the enemy King.
questions.hintText: Ask what stands on the 7th rank at the start of a game, and where the enemy King sits.

packs.title: Quant Trader Speed Mental Math
packs.subtitle: High-speed probability, compound mental arithmetic & number theory
packs.author: Jane Street Prep Cohort

questions.question: Compute 35² (35 × 35) mentally.
questions.explanation: To square any number ending in 5: multiply the first digit n by (n+1), then append 25. 3 × 4 = 12 -> 1225.
questions.hintText: Squares of numbers ending in 5 have a shortcut: tens digit × the next digit up, then 25.

questions.question: Two fair 6-sided dice are rolled. How many of the 36 outcomes sum to exactly 7?
questions.explanation: The pairs summing to 7 are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) — exactly 6 outcomes.
questions.hintText: List the pairs in order, starting with a 1 on the first die.

questions.question: At an 8% annual compound return, approximately how many years does it take to double your portfolio?
questions.explanation: By the Rule of 72: Years to double ≈ 72 / Interest Rate = 72 / 8 = 9 years.
questions.hintText: Use the rule of 72.

questions.question: How many handshakes occur if 10 people in a room each shake hands with everyone else once?
questions.explanation: n(n - 1) / 2 = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 unique handshakes.
questions.hintText: Count each pair once: choose 2 people out of 10.

questions.question: What is 45² (45 × 45) calculated instantly?
questions.explanation: Rule for numbers ending in 5: 4 × (4 + 1) = 20, attach 25 -> 2025.
questions.hintText: Ends in 5? Multiply the tens digit by the next digit up, then put 25 on the end.

questions.question: What is 34 × 11 computed in your head?
questions.explanation: Insert sum of digits (3 + 4 = 7) between 3 and 4 -> 374.
questions.hintText: Multiplying by 11: add the two digits and write the sum between them.

questions.question: At an interest rate of 6% compounded annually, about how many years will it take for an investment to double?
questions.explanation: Rule of 72: Years = 72 / rate = 72 / 6 = 12 years.
questions.hintText: The rule of 72 gives a quick doubling time.

questions.question: What is 65² (65 × 65)?
questions.hintText: Use the ends-in-5 squaring trick: tens digit × the next digit, then 25.

questions.question: What is the probability of flipping two heads in two independent fair coin flips?
questions.hintText: Independent events: multiply their probabilities.

questions.question: What is 1200 / 25 calculated quickly?
questions.explanation: Dividing by 25 is multiplying by 4 and dividing by 100: (1200 × 4) / 100 = 4800 / 100 = 48.
questions.hintText: Think of 25 as a quarter of 100.

questions.question: What is 85² (85 × 85)?
questions.hintText: Squaring a number ending in 5: the tens digit times its successor, then 25 on the end.

questions.question: A game pays $10 with probability 0.5 and $0 with probability 0.5. What is the expected value E[X]?
questions.hintText: Weight each payout by its probability, then add.

questions.question: What is 103 × 105 computed mentally?
questions.hintText: Base-100 trick: cross-add the excess over 100, then multiply the two excesses.

questions.question: Flipping a fair coin until you see Heads. What is the EXPECTED number of flips required?
questions.explanation: For a geometric distribution with p = 0.5, expected trials E[N] = 1/p = 1/0.5 = 2 flips.
questions.hintText: The expected wait for a success is the reciprocal of its probability.

questions.question: What is 98 × 96 computed mentally?
questions.hintText: Base-100 trick: subtract one gap from the other number, then multiply the two gaps.

questions.question: What is the DELTA of a Call option that is deep in-the-money (almost certain to be exercised)?
questions.explanation: Deep in-the-money call options move dollar-for-dollar with the underlying asset, having a delta approaching +1.0.
questions.hintText: Delta is the change in the option's price per $1 move in the stock.

questions.question: What is 95² (95 × 95)?
questions.hintText: Ends-in-5 squares: tens digit times the next digit, followed by 25.

questions.question: If a bet has 60% win rate (p = 0.6) paying 1:1 (b = 1), what fraction f* of your bankroll should you bet according to Kelly (f = (bp - q) / b)?
questions.hintText: Remember q = 1 − p is the chance of losing.

questions.question: Which Greek measures the rate of decay of an option's price over time (time decay)?
questions.explanation: Theta represents the sensitivity of the option's value to the passage of time (daily decay).
questions.hintText: Options are wasting assets; this Greek is usually negative for an option you own.

questions.question: Disease affects 1% of population. Test has 90% true positive and 10% false positive. If a random person tests positive, what is the approximate probability they actually have the disease?
questions.hintText: Imagine 1000 people: how many true and how many false positives?

questions.question: The Sharpe Ratio of an investment portfolio is calculated as:
questions.optionsString: (Return - Benchmark) / Beta|(Return - Risk-Free Rate) / Volatility (σ)|Total Profit / Total Loss|Dividend Yield / Price
questions.explanation: Sharpe Ratio = (R_p - R_f) / σ_p, measuring risk-adjusted excess return per unit of volatility.
questions.hintText: Think 'reward per unit of risk', measured against a risk-free baseline.

questions.question: What is 125 × 32 computed mentally without a calculator?
questions.hintText: 125 is a neat fraction of 1000.

questions.question: In the Black-Scholes model, stock prices are assumed to follow which distribution?
questions.optionsString: Lognormal distribution (geometric Brownian motion)|Uniform distribution|Student's t-distribution with 1 degree of freedom|Binomial distribution
questions.explanation: Black-Scholes assumes underlying asset prices are lognormally distributed with constant volatility.
questions.hintText: Prices can't go negative, and they grow by percentages, not fixed amounts.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of people in a room required for the probability of at least two sharing a birthday to exceed 50%?
questions.explanation: With 23 people, there are C(23, 2) = 253 pairs; the probability of at least one shared birthday exceeds 50.7%.
questions.hintText: Count pairs of people, not people: pairs grow much faster than headcount.

questions.question: If an asset has an annual volatility of 16%, what is its daily volatility assuming 256 trading days in a year (Square Root of Time rule)?
questions.explanation: Daily σ = Annual σ / √256 = 16% / 16 = 1.0%.
questions.hintText: Volatility scales with the square root of time, not linearly.

questions.question: What is the number of distinct ways to choose 2 stocks from a universe of 20 stocks (C(20, 2))?
questions.hintText: A pair has no order: don't count A-then-B and B-then-A separately.

questions.question: What is the financial law stating that two assets with identical future cash flows must sell for the same price?
questions.optionsString: The Law of One Price|Fisher's Hypothesis|The Efficient Frontier|Pareto Optimality
questions.explanation: The Law of One Price states identical cash flows must have identical prices; otherwise, risk-free arbitrage exists.
questions.hintText: If prices differed, traders could profit with no risk.

questions.question: If customer orders arrive as a Poisson process at an average rate of λ = 3 per minute, what is the variance of the number of arrivals in one minute?
questions.explanation: In a Poisson distribution, the variance Var(X) is equal to the mean λ: Var(X) = λ = 3.
questions.hintText: Poisson counts have a famous link between variance and mean.

questions.question: What is 'slippage' in algorithmic execution?
questions.optionsString: A delay between the exchange and the trading server|The commission the broker charges for each order|The gap between an order's expected and actual fill price|A drift in the clock of the trading server hardware
questions.explanation: Slippage occurs during market volatility or latency when an order fills at a worse price than anticipated.
questions.hintText: Your order is sent at one price, but the market may move before it fills.

questions.question: If a stock falls by 50%, what percentage gain is required from the low to return to the original price?
questions.explanation: If a $100 stock drops to $50, it must gain $50 to reach $100 again. $50 / $50 = 100% gain required.
questions.hintText: Measure the gain against the new, smaller base, not the original price.

questions.question: What does Value at Risk (VaR) at 95% confidence for 1 day equal to $1,000,000 mean?
questions.optionsString: There is a 5% chance that the portfolio will lose more than $1,000,000 over the next day|The portfolio is guaranteed to make $1,000,000 in 95 days|The maximum loss possible is exactly $1,000,000|The portfolio has a 95% chance of zero loss
questions.explanation: 95% 1-day VaR means that in 95 out of 100 days losses will not exceed $1M (5% tail risk).
questions.hintText: Read it as a percentile of daily losses: how often are days worse than this?

questions.question: In the St. Petersburg game, the payout doubles on every coin flip (2, 4, 8, 16...). What is the theoretical expected value?
questions.explanation: Sum (1/2)^k × 2^k = 1 + 1 + 1 + ... = Infinity (St. Petersburg paradox).
questions.hintText: Write out probability × payout for the first few rounds and look at the pattern.

questions.question: For European options on non-dividend stock, what fundamental relationship links Call (C) and Put (P) with Strike K and Stock S?
questions.optionsString: C + P = S + K × e^(-rT)|C - P = S - K × e^(-rT)|C - P = S + K × e^(-rT)|C × P = S × K × e^(-rT)
questions.explanation: Put-Call Parity: C - P = S - K × e^(-rT) (or C + K×e^(-rT) = P + S).
questions.hintText: Two portfolios with identical payoffs at expiry must cost the same today.

packs.title: Astrophysics & Relativistic Mechanics
packs.subtitle: Escape velocity, orbital resonances, thermodynamics & photon energy
packs.author: CERN Open Curricula

questions.question: Approximately how many minutes does it take sunlight to travel 1 AU from the Sun to Earth?
questions.explanation: At c ≈ 300,000 km/s across 150 million km, light takes ~500 seconds ≈ 8.3 minutes.
questions.hintText: Time = distance ÷ speed; light covers about 300,000 km every second.

questions.question: If the distance between two masses is tripled (3r), by what factor does their gravitational attraction decrease (1/N)? Enter N:
questions.explanation: Newton's Universal Gravitation follows an inverse-square law (1/r²). Tripling r reduces force by 3² = 9.
questions.hintText: Gravity follows an inverse-square law: F ∝ 1/r².

questions.question: Earth's escape velocity is approximately how many km/s (rounded to the nearest integer)?
questions.explanation: v_escape = sqrt(2GM/R) ≈ 11.2 km/s (rounded to 11 km/s).
questions.hintText: Escape speed is √2 times the circular-orbit speed near the surface.

questions.question: What optical shift in light spectra proved to Edwin Hubble that distant galaxies are moving away from us?
questions.explanation: Light from receding galaxies is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths (redshift) as space expands; farther galaxies show a bigger shift.
questions.hintText: Think of a siren dropping in pitch as the ambulance drives away: the same effect for light.

questions.question: According to Planck's relation, the energy of a photon is directly proportional to its:
questions.explanation: Planck's equation states that photon energy E equals Planck's constant h multiplied by its frequency f.
questions.hintText: Compare the energy of a gamma-ray photon with that of a radio photon.

questions.question: What is the Chandrasekhar limit (~1.4 solar masses)?
questions.optionsString: The minimum mass a gas cloud needs to ignite hydrogen fusion|The maximum mass a white dwarf can have and stay stable|The maximum mass of a neutron star before it collapses further|The upper mass limit of stars on the main sequence
questions.explanation: Above ~1.4 solar masses, electron degeneracy pressure cannot prevent gravitational collapse in a white dwarf.
questions.hintText: It marks where electron degeneracy pressure stops holding a stellar remnant up.

questions.question: In General Relativity, how does time pass near a massive body (like a neutron star or black hole) compared to deep empty space?
questions.optionsString: Time passes SLOWER near the massive object|Time passes FASTER near the massive object|Time flows in reverse|Time is completely unaffected by gravity
questions.explanation: Stronger gravitational potential slows down proper time relative to a distant observer (gravitational time dilation).
questions.hintText: Think of GPS: satellite clocks need correcting because gravity is weaker up there.

questions.question: What is the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation with temperature ~2.725 Kelvin?
questions.optionsString: Microwaves emitted by microwave ovens|Thermal radiation released ~380,000 years after the Big Bang|Light from nearby stars reflecting off asteroid dust|Signals from communication satellites
questions.explanation: The CMB is ancient relic radiation from the recombination era when the universe first became transparent to light.
questions.hintText: It reaches us evenly from every direction in the sky, not from any single source.

questions.question: What is the Schwarzschild radius of a non-rotating mass M (formula for the event horizon radius)?
questions.optionsString: r_s = GM / c²|r_s = 2GM / c²|r_s = GM / 2c²|r_s = √(2GM / c)
questions.explanation: The Schwarzschild radius is r_s = 2GM / c², setting escape velocity equal to the speed of light c.
questions.hintText: Derived from ½mv² = GMm/r when v = c.

questions.question: For which breakthrough discovery did Albert Einstein win the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921?
questions.optionsString: Special Relativity (E = mc²)|General Relativity (Curved spacetime)|Explanation of the Photoelectric Effect using light quanta (photons)|Bose-Einstein Condensation
questions.explanation: Einstein was awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize for his law of the photoelectric effect, establishing the quantum nature of light.
questions.hintText: The committee did not cite either of his relativity theories.

questions.question: How do atomic nuclei fuse inside the Sun despite their mutual electrostatic Coulomb repulsion?
questions.optionsString: Quantum tunneling through the Coulomb barrier|The Sun has a gigantic mechanical compressor|Protons lose their electric charge at 10 million Kelvin|Magnetic field eliminates all electric repulsion
questions.explanation: The core of the Sun (~15M K) is not hot enough for classical fusion; quantum tunneling allows protons to overcome the Coulomb barrier.
questions.hintText: Classically the protons are too slow; think of what wave-like particles can do at a barrier.

questions.question: What did Albert Einstein famously call quantum entanglement due to its non-local correlation across space?
questions.optionsString: Cosmic harmony|Spooky action at a distance|The holographic mirror|Wavefunction hallucination
questions.explanation: Einstein was uncomfortable with instantaneous non-local state collapse and called it 'spooky action at a distance'.
questions.hintText: He objected that it seemed to need instant influence across distance.

questions.question: What relates the wavelength λ of any matter particle to its linear momentum p (p = m·v)?
questions.optionsString: λ = p / h|λ = h·p|λ = h / p|λ = p² / 2m
questions.explanation: De Broglie's matter wave equation states λ = h / p, where h is Planck's constant and p is momentum.
questions.hintText: Check units: h is in J·s, p in kg·m/s, and λ must come out as a length.

questions.question: What is the theoretical radiation that black holes are predicted to emit due to quantum vacuum fluctuations near the event horizon?
questions.explanation: Stephen Hawking showed in 1974 that quantum particle-antiparticle pairs near the horizon cause black holes to slowly radiate and evaporate.
questions.hintText: A 1974 prediction linking quantum theory, gravity and heat; named after its author.

questions.question: What do experimental violations of Bell's inequalities definitively prove about our universe?
questions.optionsString: The universe cannot be both local and realistic|The speed of light can be exceeded by spaceships|Electrons do not possess spin|Gravity does not exist at micro-scales
questions.explanation: Bell proved that local hidden-variable theories must obey an inequality; experiments (Clauser, Aspect, Zeilinger) violate it, so nature cannot be both local and realistic.
questions.hintText: Ask which of Einstein's assumptions about particles in the EPR argument the experiments undermine.

questions.question: As a particle with mass approaches the speed of light (v -> c), what happens to its relativistic momentum and energy?
questions.optionsString: They remain constant|They drop to zero|They grow without limit, approaching infinity|They turn negative
questions.explanation: The Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 - v²/c²) diverges to infinity as v approaches c, preventing any mass from reaching c.
questions.hintText: Look at γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) as v gets close to c.

questions.question: What outward quantum pressure halts the gravitational collapse in a neutron star?
questions.optionsString: Thermal gas pressure|Neutron degeneracy pressure|Electron repulsion|Electromagnetic radiation pressure
questions.explanation: Neutron degeneracy pressure, governed by the Pauli Exclusion Principle for fermions, supports the neutron star against gravity.
questions.hintText: A purely quantum effect: it would persist even if the star cooled to absolute zero.

questions.question: How does Einstein's theory of gravity describe the gravitational orbit of Earth around the Sun?
questions.optionsString: Earth follows a geodesic in spacetime curved by the Sun's mass|An invisible magnetic tether pulls Earth|Subatomic gravitons physically push Earth like wind|Earth is suspended in liquid ether
questions.explanation: Mass tells spacetime how to curve; spacetime tells mass how to move along geodesics.
questions.hintText: In general relativity gravity is geometry, not a pulling force: Earth moves freely.

questions.question: What percentage of the total mass-energy budget of the observable universe is estimated to consist of Dark Energy?
questions.explanation: Dark Energy constitutes ~68%, Dark Matter ~27%, and ordinary baryonic matter is only about 5%.
questions.hintText: Ordinary matter, dark matter and dark energy must add up to 100%.

questions.question: What is the spin quantum number of all fermions (such as electrons, quarks, protons, and neutrons)?
questions.explanation: Fermions obey Fermi-Dirac statistics and possess half-integer spin (electrons have spin 1/2). Bosons have integer spin.
questions.hintText: Take the electron's spin and generalise; bosons such as the photon have spin 1.

questions.question: What is the heaviest chemical element that can be produced in the core of a massive star via exothermic nuclear fusion before it collapses into a supernova?
questions.explanation: Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon; fusing iron absorbs energy rather than releasing it, triggering gravitational collapse.
questions.hintText: Look for the nucleus with the highest binding energy per nucleon.

questions.question: Why can NO object with mass reach or exceed the speed of light in vacuum?
questions.optionsString: Reaching c would require infinite energy|Friction with dark matter halts it|Light photons block its path physically|Its size expands beyond the universe
questions.explanation: As v approaches c, gamma factor γ = 1/√(1 - v²/c²) approaches infinity, demanding infinite work.
questions.hintText: Think about how much energy each extra bit of speed costs as you near c.

questions.question: What happens when light from a distant quasar passes close to a massive galaxy cluster?
questions.optionsString: The light slows down to a complete halt|The light's path bends, giving magnified or multiple images|The light is converted into radio waves|The light turns into dark matter
questions.explanation: Gravitational lensing acts as a cosmic magnifying glass, bending photon trajectories around massive spacetime distortions.
questions.hintText: In general relativity light follows the geometry of spacetime; massive objects change that geometry.

questions.question: What does the Second Law of Thermodynamics imply about the ultimate fate of the universe in the 'Heat Death' scenario?
questions.optionsString: Entropy will decrease to zero|Entropy will reach a maximum, leaving no usable energy|All stars will re-ignite simultaneously|The temperature will reach infinity
questions.explanation: At maximum cosmic entropy, all energy is evenly distributed at uniform temperature, ending all thermodynamic work.
questions.hintText: Entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease; where does it end up in the long run?

questions.question: In the Schrödinger's Cat thought experiment, what causes the cat's state to resolve from a superposition to a definite outcome in the Copenhagen interpretation?
questions.optionsString: Decoherence by heat|The passage of 1 hour|The act of measurement (wavefunction collapse)|Nuclear decay
questions.explanation: In the Copenhagen interpretation, physical measurement collapses the wave function |ψ⟩ into an eigenstate.
questions.hintText: In the Copenhagen view the state stays undefined until a particular kind of act is done to it.

questions.question: What does Hubble's Constant H₀ measure?
questions.optionsString: The expansion rate of the universe (~70 km/s per Mpc)|The total mass of the Milky Way|The temperature of the sun's corona|The speed of gravitational waves
questions.explanation: Hubble's constant relates recession velocity to distance: v = H₀ × d, measuring cosmic expansion.
questions.hintText: Hubble's law is v = H₀·d: think about what v and d stand for.
questions.acceptedAnswers: Expansion rate|Expansion rate of the universe

questions.question: What fundamental property does the Higgs field impart to elementary particles (like quarks and W/Z bosons) through their interaction with it?
questions.optionsString: Electric charge|Rest mass|Color charge|Magnetic dipole moment
questions.explanation: Particles gain inertial mass through the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism by interacting with the non-zero vacuum expectation value of the Higgs field.
questions.hintText: Compare the W and Z bosons, which feel this field, with the photon, which does not.

questions.question: What minute anomaly in Mercury's orbit could NOT be explained by Newtonian gravity, but was precisely predicted by Einstein's General Relativity?
questions.optionsString: Its orbital period was slowing down|Perihelion precession of 43 arcseconds per century|Its orbit was becoming more circular|Its axial tilt was changing
questions.explanation: The curvature of spacetime near the Sun accounts for the extra 43 arcseconds per century in Mercury's perihelion shift.
questions.hintText: It concerns Mercury's elliptical orbit and how it slowly shifts over centuries.
questions.acceptedAnswers: Perihelion precession|Precession of the perihelion|Perihelion shift

questions.question: Gravitational waves, directly detected by LIGO in 2015 from colliding black holes, propagate through space at what speed?
questions.optionsString: The speed of light in vacuum (c)|Infinite speed|Speed of sound|Half the speed of light
questions.explanation: In General Relativity, ripples in the curvature of spacetime propagate at exactly the speed of light c.
questions.hintText: A 2017 neutron-star merger was seen in gravitational waves and gamma rays: compare arrival times.
questions.acceptedAnswers: Speed of light|The speed of light|Light speed

questions.question: What virtual force-carrier particle mediates the electromagnetic force between charged particles in QED?
questions.explanation: In quantum electrodynamics (QED), electromagnetic interactions occur through the exchange of virtual photons.
questions.hintText: In QED the carrier is the quantum of the electromagnetic field itself: what do lamps emit?

questions.question: What is the fundamental physical significance of the Planck Length (~1.616 × 10⁻³⁵ meters)?
questions.optionsString: The size of a hydrogen atom|The diameter of a quark|The scale where quantum gravity effects dominate|The wavelength of visible light
questions.explanation: Below the Planck scale, quantum fluctuations of spacetime geometry become so severe that smooth manifolds cease to exist.
questions.hintText: It is built from just three constants: G, ħ and c.

questions.question: What bizarre macroscopic quantum state occurs when bosons are cooled to temperatures within nanokelvins of absolute zero?
questions.optionsString: They vaporize explosively|Atoms occupy one ground state and act as a single wave|They turn into antimatter|Their mass becomes infinite
questions.explanation: In a BEC, millions of bosons lose individual identity and merge into a coherent macroscopic quantum super-atom.
questions.hintText: Bosons may all share one quantum state: what happens when they all do?

questions.question: What fundamental quantum rule dictates that no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state simultaneously?
questions.optionsString: Heisenberg's matrix|The Pauli Exclusion Principle|Fermi's golden rule|Newton's 3rd law
questions.explanation: Wolfgang Pauli showed that multi-fermion wavefunctions must be anti-symmetric under particle exchange, giving matter stability and volume.
questions.hintText: It explains why electrons fill atomic shells instead of all sitting in the lowest level.

packs.title: Big Tech Systems & Algorithmic Mastery
packs.subtitle: Graph theory, concurrency, memory complexity & Kotlin/Python internals
packs.author: Systems Architecture Guild

questions.question: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height H=3 (where a single root node has height 1)?
questions.explanation: A full binary tree of height H has 2^H - 1 nodes. For H=3: 2³ - 1 = 7 nodes.
questions.hintText: Count level by level; each level has twice as many nodes as the one above.

questions.question: Which data structure guarantees O(1) average-time lookup AND preserves insertion order in Kotlin/Java?
questions.explanation: LinkedHashMap maintains a doubly-linked list running through its hash buckets, giving O(1) lookup with predictable insertion order.
questions.hintText: Hashing alone loses the order; something must remember it too.

questions.question: In distributed systems, the CAP Theorem states a system during a network partition (P) must trade off between:
questions.explanation: Brewer's CAP Theorem states that in the presence of a Network Partition (P), a distributed data store must choose between Consistency (C) and Availability (A).
questions.hintText: A cut-off node can answer anyway, or wait until it can check with its peers.

questions.question: What is the optimal time complexity of comparison-based sorting (like MergeSort) in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Mathematically proven via decision trees: comparison-based sorts require Ω(n log n) operations in the worst case.
questions.hintText: Picture a decision tree with n! leaves: its height is the worst-case number of comparisons.

questions.question: Which graph search algorithm uses a Queue and explores level-by-level to guarantee the shortest path in unweighted graphs?
questions.optionsString: Breadth-First Search (BFS)|Depth-First Search (DFS)|Dijkstra's with negative weights|Topological Sort
questions.explanation: BFS traverses nodes layer by layer using a FIFO queue, finding shortest paths on unweighted graphs.
questions.hintText: Think of ripples on water: all nodes at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on.

questions.question: An In-Order traversal (Left -> Node -> Right) on a valid Binary Search Tree produces values in what order?
questions.explanation: In a BST, Left < Node < Right; traversing In-Order inherently yields elements in sorted ascending order.
questions.hintText: Compare left subtree, node and right subtree by value, then read them in visiting order.

questions.question: What is the average-case lookup time in a well-distributed Hash Table?
questions.explanation: A hash function computes bucket index directly, offering O(1) constant average lookup time.
questions.hintText: The hash function maps the key to a bucket index; then you check only that bucket.

questions.question: What essential component must every recursive function have to prevent infinite recursion and a StackOverflowError?
questions.optionsString: Base case (termination condition)|A global variable|A while loop|A thread lock
questions.explanation: A base case returns a value without making further recursive calls, unwinding the call stack.
questions.hintText: Think of the smallest input, like factorial(0), that is answered without calling itself.

questions.question: What combination of two data structures implements an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache with O(1) get and put?
questions.optionsString: Binary Tree + Array|Hash Map + Doubly Linked List|Stack + Queue|Red-Black Tree + Heap
questions.explanation: HashMap gives O(1) key-to-node lookup, while a Doubly Linked List allows O(1) node removal and insertion to the front.
questions.hintText: One structure finds an entry by key; the other keeps entries ordered by recent use.
questions.acceptedAnswers: Hash Map + Doubly Linked List|HashMap + Doubly Linked List|Hash table + doubly linked list

questions.question: Which greedy algorithm finds the single-source shortest paths in a directed graph with NON-NEGATIVE edge weights?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm uses a priority queue to iteratively expand the closest unvisited node on graphs with non-negative weights.
questions.hintText: Each step, settle the unvisited node with the smallest known distance from the source.

questions.question: What two core properties indicate that a problem is best solved using Dynamic Programming?
questions.optionsString: Optimal Substructure and Overlapping Subproblems|Randomized Inputs and Infinite Recursion|Sorted arrays and Prime factors|Greedy Choice and Constant Time
questions.explanation: DP applies when an optimal solution can be constructed from optimal solutions to overlapping subproblems.
questions.hintText: In naive recursive Fibonacci, how do the subproblems relate to each other and to the answer?

questions.question: Why are Tries exceptionally well-suited for autocomplete search engines?
questions.optionsString: They always use less memory than a hash table of the same words|Finding a prefix takes O(L) steps, independent of dictionary size|They encrypt every stored word with no extra cost|They avoid pointer overhead by storing words in one array
questions.explanation: In a Trie, walking down to the node for a prefix of length L takes O(L) steps, however many million words are stored.
questions.hintText: Count the steps needed to follow a prefix's characters down from the root.

questions.question: In the famous 'Two Sum II' problem on a SORTED array, how do two pointers find the target sum in O(n) time and O(1) space?
questions.optionsString: Sort the array first, then check every pair in order|Start both pointers at index 0 and move them right together|Pointers at both ends: sum too small, move left up; too big, move right down|Check every pair of elements using two nested loops
questions.explanation: Because the array is sorted, incrementing left increases the sum, and decrementing right decreases the sum.
questions.hintText: Sorted order tells you how each pointer move changes the sum. Where should they start?

questions.question: What is the optimal time complexity to find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of fixed size K in an array of size N?
questions.explanation: Using sliding window, each step subtracts the element leaving the window and adds the entering element in O(1), making total time O(N).
questions.hintText: Add the incoming element and subtract the outgoing element at each step.

questions.question: What does the Atomic Compare-And-Swap (CAS) instruction enable in lock-free multi-threaded data structures?
questions.optionsString: Atomic updates without mutexes, retrying on conflict|Deliberately slowing threads down to avoid races|Deleting unreachable memory automatically|Doubling the effective CPU cache size
questions.explanation: CAS atomically compares memory location against expected value and updates if matched, enabling lock-free algorithms.
questions.hintText: Read the old value, compute the new one, then write only if nothing changed meanwhile.

questions.question: With both 'Union by Rank' and 'Path Compression' heuristics, what is the nearly constant amortized time complexity per operation?
questions.explanation: Path compression + rank union yields O(α(n)) amortized per operation, where α(n) < 5 for all practical universe sizes.
questions.hintText: Think of a function that grows so slowly it stays tiny for any input that fits in memory.

questions.question: What is the fundamental rationale behind the 'Generational Hypothesis' utilized by modern Garbage Collectors (G1, ZGC)?
questions.optionsString: All objects live forever|Most objects die shortly after creation (infant mortality)|Objects never move between heap areas|Strings take 90% of heap
questions.explanation: Empirical studies prove that the vast majority of allocated objects become garbage very quickly, justifying young/old generational separation.
questions.hintText: Think of temporary objects, like loop variables and short-lived strings: how long do they live?

questions.question: Which distributed consensus algorithm do etcd (used by Kubernetes) and HashiCorp Consul rely on?
questions.explanation: Raft is designed for understandability while providing full Paxos-equivalent consensus for leader election and replicated state machines.
questions.hintText: It was designed as an easier-to-understand alternative to Paxos.

questions.question: What is the time complexity to find the Longest Common Prefix of N strings each of maximum length L using a Trie?
questions.explanation: Inserting N strings takes O(N × L), and traversing down the single-child branch takes O(L) time, giving O(N × L) total.
questions.hintText: Which step costs more: building the trie, or walking down the shared single-child path?

questions.question: Why do modern 64-bit CPU architectures pad struct/class fields to multiples of 4 or 8 bytes?
questions.optionsString: To make reverse-engineering and decompiling harder|Aligned accesses take one memory cycle; unaligned ones may need several|Memory chips physically cannot store data at odd addresses|To stop buffer overflows from corrupting adjacent fields
questions.explanation: CPUs access memory efficiently at aligned word boundaries (e.g. 64-bit words); unaligned access penalizes throughput.
questions.hintText: Consider what happens when a 4-byte value straddles two 8-byte words.

questions.question: On which type of graph is Topological Sort strictly guaranteed to be possible?
questions.optionsString: Any undirected graph|Graphs with negative cycles|Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)|Complete bipartite graphs only
questions.explanation: Topological sort is possible if and only if the directed graph has NO cycles (it is a DAG).
questions.hintText: Think of course prerequisites: what would a circular dependency do to the ordering?

questions.question: What type of error can a standard Bloom Filter produce?
questions.optionsString: False Negatives only|False Positives only|Both False Positives and False Negatives|Zero errors ever
questions.explanation: A Bloom filter guarantees no false negatives: if it says 'not present', it is definitely not. But hash collisions can yield false positives.
questions.hintText: Different items can set the same bits; what does that do to a lookup for an item never added?

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the standard dynamic-programming solution to the 0/1 Knapsack Problem with N items and maximum weight capacity W?
questions.explanation: The standard DP table has dimensions (N + 1) × (W + 1), evaluated in pseudo-polynomial O(N × W) time.
questions.hintText: Count the subproblems: each is defined by the items considered so far and the remaining capacity.

questions.question: What is 'Thrashing' in virtual memory systems?
questions.optionsString: A hard drive vibrating physically under heavy read/write load|Constant paging between RAM and disk that leaves the CPU little time for real work|Network packet loss rising above 50% of all traffic|Threads being created and deleted too rapidly
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when high memory pressure causes continuous page faults, grinding the system to a halt.
questions.hintText: What happens when the working sets of all running programs do not fit in RAM together?

questions.question: What bytecode transformation does the Kotlin compiler apply to an `inline` function with reified type parameters?
questions.optionsString: Generates a separate subclass for every type argument used|Falls back to runtime reflection on every single call|Inlines the function body at each call site, substituting the actual type|Compiles the function into native C++ code before packaging
questions.explanation: Inlining copies the bytecode directly into the call site, allowing exact type access despite JVM type erasure.
questions.hintText: JVM generics are erased at runtime, so the real type must be baked into the code at compile time.

questions.question: What is the main operational advantage of a B-Tree over a Red-Black Tree in database indexing (e.g. Postgres / SQLite)?
questions.optionsString: Wide nodes, one per disk page, mean far fewer disk reads per lookup|B-Trees avoid storing any pointers between nodes|B-Trees are unable to store duplicate keys|Red-Black trees cannot be kept balanced after inserts
questions.explanation: B-Trees have wide nodes matching disk page sizes (4KB-16KB), drastically reducing expensive disk seeks.
questions.hintText: Disk reads are slow and happen a whole page at a time. How many keys can one page hold?

questions.question: What fast operation checks if a positive integer N is an exact power of 2 (e.g. 2, 4, 8, 16)?
questions.explanation: Powers of 2 have only 1 bit set (e.g. 1000₂). N - 1 has all lower bits set (0111₂). (N & (N - 1)) == 0.
questions.hintText: A power of 2 has a single 1 bit; subtracting 1 flips that bit and every bit below it.

questions.question: What concurrency anomaly occurs when Transaction A reads a row, Transaction B updates that row and commits, and Transaction A reads it again getting different values?
questions.explanation: A Non-Repeatable Read occurs when re-reading the same committed row produces modified data.
questions.hintText: Think about what changed between the two reads: an existing row's value, or the set of rows?
questions.acceptedAnswers: Non-Repeatable Read|Nonrepeatable Read|Non Repeatable Read|Fuzzy Read

questions.question: Why does TCP establish connections using a 3-Way Handshake (SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK)?
questions.optionsString: To synchronize sequence numbers and confirm both sides can send and receive|To encrypt all payload data before it leaves the host|To assign an IP address dynamically to the client|To prevent physical interference on the network wire
questions.explanation: The 3-way handshake verifies both endpoints can send and receive, agreeing on initial packet sequence numbers.
questions.hintText: Picture the three messages: each side announces something and the other acknowledges it.

questions.question: Which dispatcher should be used in Kotlin for offloading disk I/O or network API requests to prevent blocking the UI thread?
questions.explanation: Dispatchers.IO uses an elastic thread pool specifically designed for blocking I/O calls.
questions.hintText: Think about threads that mostly sit waiting for a disk or a server instead of computing.

questions.question: How does Consistent Hashing minimize data movement when a new caching node is added to a distributed cluster of N nodes?
questions.optionsString: It rehashes every key onto the new node layout|It deletes the oldest keys to make room|Keys and nodes sit on a hash ring, so only keys next to the new node move|It stores every key on every node
questions.explanation: On a hash ring, a new node only takes over keys from its immediate successor (about 1/N of all keys); all other keys stay where they are.
questions.hintText: With hash(key) mod N, changing N moves almost every key. What layout avoids that?

questions.question: What is 'False Sharing' in high-performance multi-threaded C++/Java applications?
questions.optionsString: Independent variables written by different threads that sit on one 64-byte cache line|Two threads writing the same variable without any synchronization|A memory leak caused by objects that are shared between threads|Threads holding separate copies of an object while assuming it is shared
questions.explanation: False sharing occurs when independent variables sit on the same cache line, forcing L1/L2 cache coherence invalidations.
questions.hintText: Think about the unit in which CPU caches move memory between cores: not single variables.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) problem using binary search with patience sorting?
questions.explanation: Patience sorting maintains an active array of smallest tails and updates it via binary search in O(n log n) time.
questions.hintText: One binary search over the sorted tails per element; add up the cost over all n elements.

packs.subtitle: Nash equilibria, Bayesian puzzles, Monty Hall & deduction
